## `singular_plural_type_mismatch` findings in `src/api/state.ts`

Only one finding hits this file — `crime_00033`, covering two declarations on lines 24 and 27.

### Evidence (verbatim from the finding)

> - "plural name, singular type: `users: User` @L24"
> - "singular name, array type: `invoice: Invoice[]` @L27"
> - "v1 detector — type aliases and generic types are silently skipped"

### Declaration 1 — `users: User` @ L24

```ts
export const users: User = { id: "u_1", email: "a@b.c" };
```

**Proposal: rename to `user`.** The initializer is a single object literal with one `id` and one `email`. The *type* (`User`) and the *value* (one object) both describe a single record; only the variable name disagrees. The type carries the intended meaning — rename the binding to `user` (matching the negative-control on L33).

### Declaration 2 — `invoice: Invoice[]` @ L27

```ts
export const invoice: Invoice[] = [];
```

**Proposal: rename to `invoices`.** The annotation is explicitly `Invoice[]` and the initializer is an array literal. Both the type and the value shape say "many," so the type carries the intended meaning here too — rename the binding to `invoices` (matching the negative-control on L34).

### Why "rename" both times rather than retype either

In each case there are two signals pointing one way (the type annotation + the initializer shape) and one signal pointing the other way (the identifier). When two out of three agree, the dissenting one is almost always the typo — and here the negative controls a few lines below (`user: User`, `invoices: Invoice[]`) confirm that the file's author already knows the correct conventions; L24 and L27 are slips.

Renames are also the lower-risk edit: changing the type would force every consumer to adapt to a different shape, while renaming a binding only touches imports.
